decks.title: Market Equilibrium — Part 1: Equilibrium and Single Shifts
goals: Define equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity
Explain how excess demand and excess supply move the price to equilibrium
Describe the invisible hand in general terms
Find the effect of a shift of demand or of supply on equilibrium, with a fixed number of firms

slides.heading: Market Equilibrium: Where Demand Meets Supply
slides.body_md: Part 1 — equilibrium, the gaps away from it, and the effect of a **shift** of demand or supply.

visual.alt: Route map of part 1: market equilibrium, excess demand and excess supply, the invisible hand, shifts of demand and supply
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In a market, buyers and sellers decide together how much is bought and at what price. This part defines the balance point of a market, shows how excess demand and excess supply push the price towards it, and studies what happens when the demand or the supply changes, with the number of firms fixed.

slides.heading: Market equilibrium
slides.body_md: The **equilibrium price** is the price at which **quantity demanded equals quantity supplied**. The quantity traded at that price is the **equilibrium quantity**.

rows: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
The quantity bought and sold at the equilibrium price
No buyer who wishes to buy at that price is turned away, and no seller is left with unsold stock
A perfectly competitive market with a fixed number of firms

visual.alt: Table of definitions: equilibrium price, equilibrium quantity, market clearing and the setting of a fixed number of firms
visual.caption: Market equilibrium.

slides.narration: Equilibrium is the price at which the quantity buyers wish to buy is exactly the quantity sellers wish to sell. The market clears: nobody who wants to buy at that price is turned away and no seller is left with unsold stock. This chapter studies perfect competition with a fixed number of firms.

slides.heading: The mango market of Ratnapuri
slides.body_md: Compare quantity demanded and quantity supplied at each price. The gap shows which way the price will move.

visual.caption: Imagined Ratnapuri mango market: demand qd = 200 − 5p, supply qs = 20 + 4p.

slides.narration: On the graph the demand curve falls and the supply curve rises. They cross at the equilibrium, price 20 rupees and quantity 100 quintals. At ten rupees the supply curve lies to the left of the demand curve, so there is excess demand of 90. At thirty rupees the demand curve is on the left, so there is excess supply of 90.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: finding the equilibrium
slides.body_md: Buyers demand **qd = 200 − 5p**; sellers supply **qs = 20 + 4p**.
bullets: Step 1 — Set qd = qs: 200 − 5p = 20 + 4p.
Step 2 — Collect terms: 180 = 9p, so **p = 20**.
Step 3 — Put p into demand: q = 200 − 5 × 20 = **100**, and supply gives the same.

visual.alt: Worked table: equating demand and supply gives a price of 20 rupees per kg and a quantity of 100 quintals, confirmed by supply
visual.caption: Imagined Ratnapuri mangoes.

slides.narration: To find equilibrium, set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied. Here 200 minus 5 times the price equals 20 plus 4 times the price. Collecting terms gives 180 equals 9 times the price, so the price is 20. Putting it into demand gives 100 quintals, and supply agrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: price below equilibrium
slides.body_md: Decide what the price will do.

visual.alt: Table of the Ratnapuri mango market at 10 rupees: quantity demanded 150, quantity supplied 60, excess demand 90
visual.caption: Imagined Ratnapuri mangoes.

slides.narration: Look at the figures at ten rupees. Compare how much buyers want with how much sellers offer. Ask which side is short, and then what that side will do to the price. Pick the option that gives both the direction and the correct size of the gap.

slides.heading: Excess demand: a price below equilibrium
slides.body_md: When **quantity demanded > quantity supplied**, buyers cannot all be served, so the price **rises**.

nodes.label: Buyers compete and bid the price up
Price rises; the gap narrows to zero

visual.alt: Flow from a price below equilibrium to excess demand, to buyers bidding the price up, to a rising price and a narrowing gap
visual.caption: Excess demand

slides.narration: If the price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer. This is excess demand. Buyers who cannot get the good are ready to pay more, and sellers see that they can ask for more. The price therefore rises. As it rises, buyers want less and sellers offer more, so the gap narrows until it disappears.

slides.heading: Excess supply: a price above equilibrium
slides.body_md: When **quantity supplied > quantity demanded**, sellers are left with unsold stock, so the price **falls**.

nodes.label: Sellers with unsold stock cut the price
Price falls; the gap narrows to zero

visual.alt: Flow from a price above equilibrium to excess supply, to sellers cutting the price, to a falling price and a narrowing gap
visual.caption: Excess supply

slides.narration: If the price is above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want. This is excess supply. Sellers with unsold goods compete for buyers by cutting the price. As the price falls, buyers want more and sellers offer less, so the gap narrows until the market clears at the equilibrium price.

slides.heading: Quick check: the steps of adjustment
slides.body_md: Arrange the steps from a low price to equilibrium.

rows: Excess demand: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Excess supply: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded

visual.alt: Table of the three cases: price below equilibrium gives excess demand and a rising price, price at equilibrium gives no change, price above gives excess supply and a falling price
visual.caption: Out of equilibrium.

slides.narration: Start from a price below equilibrium. Ask what gap opens up at that price, then what the buyers do about it, and finally what happens to the gap as the price changes. Put the four steps in the order in which they occur.

slides.heading: The invisible hand
slides.body_md: Price moves to equilibrium through the **separate decisions of many buyers and sellers**, with no authority directing it.

nodes.label: Market clears with no central planner

visual.alt: Flow of the invisible hand: many buyers and sellers choose for themselves, competition moves the price, and the market clears without a central planner
visual.caption: The invisible hand

slides.narration: Economists describe this adjustment with the image of an invisible hand. No single person sets the market clearing price. Each buyer and each seller decides for himself or herself, and competition for scarce goods or for customers moves the price to the level at which the market clears.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the tomato market of Meghgaon
slides.body_md: Find the equilibrium from the schedule and the pressure on price at the other prices.
bullets: Step 1 — Scan for the row where demand equals supply: **Rs 14**, both **170** quintals.
Step 2 — At Rs 10: 230 − 110 = **120** excess demand, so the price rises.
Step 3 — At Rs 18: 230 − 110 = **120** excess supply, so the price falls.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined Meghgaon tomato market: equilibrium at 14 rupees where demand and supply are both 170; excess +180, +120, +60, 0, −60, −120 across the prices 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18
visual.caption: Imagined Meghgaon tomatoes (quintals a day).

slides.narration: Read down the schedule until the two quantities are equal. That is at 14 rupees, where both are 170 quintals. At 10 rupees demand exceeds supply by 120, so the price will rise. At 18 rupees supply exceeds demand by 120, so the price will fall.

slides.heading: Quick check: excess demand
slides.body_md: Compute the excess demand at Rs 10 per kg.

slides.narration: Work out the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied at the given price from the two functions. Subtract supply from demand. The answer is the excess demand, in quintals. You can check it against the table.

slides.heading: A fixed number of firms
slides.body_md: In this chapter the **number of firms is fixed**, so supply responds only through the price. With free entry and exit, price tends to the minimum average cost in the long run.

rows: Price and quantity, as demand and supply shift
Long run, free entry and exit
Price tends to the minimum average cost

visual.alt: Table comparing the short run with a fixed number of firms, in which price and quantity adjust, and the long run with free entry and exit, in which price tends to the minimum average cost
visual.caption: Fixed number of firms.

slides.narration: We study the short run, in which the number of firms cannot change. Price and quantity then adjust only as demand and supply shift. In the long run, if firms can enter and leave freely, the price tends towards the lowest point of average cost, but that story belongs to a later study.

slides.heading: A rise in demand
slides.body_md: If demand rises by **45** at every price, there is excess demand at the old price of 20, so the price rises.

visual.alt: Table of the Ratnapuri mango market after demand rises by 45: at 15, 20, 25, 30 rupees new demand is 170, 145, 120, 95 against supply 80, 100, 120, 140, so the market clears at 25 rupees
visual.caption: Imagined Ratnapuri mangoes (quintals a day).

slides.narration: Suppose a rise in incomes adds 45 quintals to demand at every price. At the old price of 20 rupees, demand is now 145 against supply of 100. The price rises. It settles at 25 rupees, where demand and supply are both 120 quintals.

slides.heading: A rise in demand and a rise in supply
slides.body_md: Rise in demand: price **up**, quantity **up**. Rise in supply: price **down**, quantity **up**.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: cement demand rises
slides.body_md: Sagarpur cement: **qd = 1800 − 3p**, **qs = −200 + 2p**; demand then rises by 300.
bullets: Step 1 — New demand: 2100 − 3p.
Step 2 — Equate with supply: 2300 = 5p, so **p = 460**.
Step 3 — Quantity: 2100 − 3 × 460 = **720**; the price and quantity both rise.

slides.heading: All four single shifts
slides.body_md: A shift of **demand** moves price and quantity in the **same** direction; a shift of **supply** moves them in **opposite** directions.

visual.alt: Table of the four single shifts in the Ratnapuri mango market: demand rising gives 25 and 120, demand falling gives 15 and 80, supply rising gives 15 and 125, supply falling gives 25 and 75
visual.caption: Imagined Ratnapuri mangoes; starting point Rs 20, 100 quintals.

slides.narration: Look at the four cases together. A rise in demand raises both price and quantity. A fall in demand lowers both. A rise in supply lowers the price but raises the quantity. A fall in supply raises the price but lowers the quantity. In each case the equilibrium moves along the curve that has not shifted.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

visual.alt: Summary table of part 1: equilibrium, excess demand, excess supply, effects of a rise in demand and a rise in supply, and the fixed number of firms

slides.narration: To recap. Equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. A price below it causes excess demand and the price rises; a price above it causes excess supply and the price falls. This adjustment is the invisible hand. With a fixed number of firms, a rise in demand raises price and quantity, and a rise in supply lowers price and raises quantity.

bullets: Define **equilibrium price** and **equilibrium quantity** in standard words.
Find equilibrium by setting **qd = qs** and showing every step.
State **excess demand** or **excess supply** with its size at the given price.
For a shift, say which curve moves, then give the new price and quantity.
Say that the **number of firms is fixed** in this chapter.
slides.narration: Some tips. Define the equilibrium price and quantity carefully. When you solve for equilibrium, set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied and show each step. State whether there is excess demand or excess supply and give its size. For a shift, say which curve moves, and then give the new price and quantity with figures.

slides.heading: When both curves shift
slides.body_md: If demand and supply both rise, **quantity rises**; the effect on **price** depends on which shift is larger.

headers: Shift of demand compared with shift of supply (both rising)

visual.alt: Table of the rule when demand and supply both rise: if demand shifts more the price rises, if the shifts are equal the price is unchanged, if supply shifts more the price falls, and quantity rises in every case
visual.caption: Both curves shift to the right.

slides.narration: When both curves shift in the same direction, the two effects on quantity add up, so the quantity rises if both rise. The two effects on price pull in opposite directions. A rise in demand pushes the price up and a rise in supply pushes it down. So the result depends on which shift is larger.

slides.heading: Consequences of a ceiling
slides.body_md: A binding ceiling leads to a **shortage**, which must be shared by **rationing** or **queues**; a **black market** and lower **quality** are possible.

sections.heading: 1. Market equilibrium
sections.body_md:
In a perfectly competitive market with a **fixed number of firms**, the **equilibrium price** is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied (qd = qs); the **equilibrium quantity** is the quantity bought and sold at that price. Both are found by setting demand equal to supply.

Example (imagined Ratnapuri mangoes): qd = 200 − 5p and qs = 20 + 4p give 180 = 9p, so p = 20 and q = 100.

key_terms.definition_md: The price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.
The quantity bought and sold at the equilibrium price.
A situation in which every buyer who wants to buy at the price can do so, and no seller is left with unsold stock.

sections.heading: 2. Excess demand, excess supply and the invisible hand
sections.body_md:
At a price **below** equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: there is **excess demand** (90 quintals at Rs 10), and competition among buyers raises the price. At a price **above** equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: there is **excess supply** (90 quintals at Rs 30), and sellers with unsold stock cut the price. In both cases the price moves towards equilibrium.

This movement, produced by the separate decisions of many buyers and sellers without central direction, is described as the work of an **invisible hand**.

key_terms.definition_md: The excess of quantity demanded over quantity supplied at a price below equilibrium.
The excess of quantity supplied over quantity demanded at a price above equilibrium.
The idea that competition among many buyers and sellers moves price to its market-clearing level without anyone directing it.

rows: Excess demand: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Excess supply: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded

sections.heading: 3. Shifts of demand or supply, with a fixed number of firms
sections.body_md:
- **Demand rises** (curve shifts right): price rises and quantity rises (20 to 25 and 100 to 120 in Ratnapuri). **Demand falls:** both fall.
- **Supply rises:** price falls and quantity rises (15 and 125). **Supply falls:** price rises and quantity falls.

A change in the good's own price is a movement along a curve; a change in income, tastes, input prices or other conditions shifts the curve.

With free entry and exit, price tends to the minimum average cost in the long run; this chapter keeps the number of firms fixed.

key_terms.definition_md: A change in the quantity demanded or supplied at every price, caused by a change in a condition other than the good’s own price.

sections.heading: 4. Simultaneous shifts
sections.body_md:
When demand and supply both shift, the outcome depends on the relative size of the shifts.

- Both rise by the same amount: price unchanged (20), quantity rises (145).
- Demand rises more than supply: price rises (25), quantity rises (165).
- Supply rises more than demand: price falls (15), quantity rises (170).
- Demand rises by 50 and supply falls by 40: price rises to 30, quantity unchanged (100).

The wage of labour is determined in the same way, where labour demand equals labour supply.

sections.heading: 5. Price ceiling
sections.body_md:
A **price ceiling** is a maximum price set by the government. It has an effect only if it is **below** the equilibrium price, where it creates **excess demand, a shortage**. Governments use ceilings on essential goods to keep them affordable. Consequences: rationing (for example by ration cards), queues, the possibility of a black market and lower quality.

Imagined Chandanpur gas cylinders: free price Rs 800, 400 cylinders. At a ceiling of Rs 600: demand 600, supply 300, shortage 300. A ceiling above 800 (for example Rs 900) has no effect.

key_terms.definition_md: A maximum price fixed by the government at which a good may be sold, normally below the equilibrium price.
The excess of quantity demanded over quantity supplied at a controlled price.
Sharing a limited supply among buyers by a rule such as a quota or ration card instead of by price.

sections.heading: 6. Price floor
sections.body_md:
A **price floor** is a minimum price set by the government. It has an effect only if it is **above** the equilibrium price, where it creates **excess supply, a surplus**. Governments use floors to support producers, for example a support price for a crop or a minimum wage. If the government buys the surplus it holds a **buffer stock**, which costs money to buy and store.

Imagined Dhanpur millet: free price Rs 40, 340 thousand kg. At a floor of Rs 50: demand 300, supply 400, surplus 100 thousand kg, costing Rs 5000 thousand to buy. A floor below Rs 40 has no effect.

key_terms.definition_md: A minimum price fixed by the government below which a good may not be sold, normally above the equilibrium price.
The excess of quantity supplied over quantity demanded at a controlled price.
A reserve of a good held by the government, for example grain bought as the surplus under a floor price.

sections.heading: 7. Minimum wage: a floor on labour
sections.body_md:
A **minimum wage** is a floor on the price of labour. In the imagined Kareempur weaving cluster the wage that clears the market is Rs 150 a day, with 300 weavers employed. A minimum wage of Rs 180 gives labour demand of 240 and labour supply of 390, so 150 weavers who would like to work are not employed. Weavers who keep their jobs gain; those who lose them, and employers paying more, lose.

Controls help some people and burden others, so their effects are weighed on both sides.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Define **equilibrium price**, **excess demand**, **excess supply**, **price ceiling** and **price floor** in standard words.
- Solve equilibrium by setting **qd = qs** and show each step.
- Excess demand = **qd − qs** below equilibrium; excess supply = **qs − qd** above it.
- Demand shifts move price and quantity the **same** way; supply shifts move them **oppositely**.
- For two shifts, compare the **sizes** before stating the price effect.
- A control binds only if the ceiling is **below** or the floor **above** equilibrium; compute the gap at the controlled price.
- Present controls neutrally: the aim, then the problem.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined mango market of Ratnapuri the price at which the quantity buyers wish to purchase exactly matches the quantity sellers wish to sell is called the

options.text_md: ceiling price
equilibrium price
floor price
marginal price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** equilibrium price. The price that clears the market, with quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied, is the equilibrium price. A ceiling and a floor are government-fixed limits, and no such thing as a marginal price is used for this meaning.

questions.stem_md: A trader studies mango sales in Ratnapuri, where p is the price in Rs per kg and quantities are in quintals a day: demand is qd = 200 − 5p and supply is qs = 20 + 4p. The price at which this market clears is

options.text_md: Rs 100 per kg
Rs 25 per kg
Rs 15 per kg
Rs 20 per kg

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Rs 20 per kg. Setting 200 − 5p equal to 20 + 4p gives 180 = 9p, so p = 20. The figure 100 is the equilibrium quantity, not a price, while 25 and 15 are prices after shifts of the curves.

questions.stem_md: At some price in the imagined candle market of Deepgaon, buyers want more candles than sellers are willing to offer. This situation is called

options.text_md: excess demand
excess supply
equilibrium
a price ceiling

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** excess demand. When quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a price, there is excess demand. Excess supply is the opposite, equilibrium has the two equal, and a ceiling is a legal limit on price rather than a market situation.

questions.stem_md: At a price of Rs 10 per kg buyers in Ratnapuri want 150 quintals of mangoes a day while sellers offer 60. The price is most likely to

options.text_md: fall, because there is excess demand of 90 quintals
rise, because there is excess supply of 90 quintals
rise, because there is excess demand of 90 quintals
stay unchanged, because sellers set prices alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** rise, because there is excess demand of 90 quintals. Buyers are short of mangoes by 150 − 60 = 90 quintals, and competing for them they bid the price up. Excess demand never pushes a price down, there is no excess supply at this price, and in a competitive market no single seller fixes the price.

questions.stem_md: Mango sellers in Ratnapuri ask Rs 30 per kg, and at that price buyers want 50 quintals while sellers bring 140. What happens next?

options.text_md: Buyers bid the price up, which moves towards equilibrium
The price stays at this level indefinitely
Unsold mangoes make sellers cut the price, which moves towards equilibrium
Quantity supplied falls to zero immediately

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Unsold mangoes make sellers cut the price, which moves towards equilibrium. Sellers are left with 90 quintals unsold, so they lower the price, and as it falls buyers buy more and sellers supply less until the two match. Bidding up is the response to excess demand. The market has no reason to rest at a price with unsold stock, and supply falls gradually, not to zero at once.

questions.stem_md: Economists say that in a competitive market the price moves towards equilibrium as if guided by an invisible hand. This phrase refers to the fact that

options.text_md: price adjusts through the independent decisions of many buyers and sellers, without any one of them directing it
a government office sets each price every morning
a single large firm decides the price for all others
prices never change in a competitive market

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** price adjusts through the independent decisions of many buyers and sellers, without any one of them directing it. Each buyer and seller acts for himself or herself, yet competition for scarce goods or for buyers moves price to the level where the market clears, with no central direction. A government office or one dominant firm setting price would not be a competitive market, and price clearly does change when there is excess demand or supply.

questions.stem_md: A burst of house building increases the demand for cement in Sagarpur at every price, while the number of cement firms stays the same. In the new equilibrium

options.text_md: price is higher but quantity is lower
price is lower but quantity is higher
both price and quantity are lower
both price and quantity are higher

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** both price and quantity are higher. The demand curve shifts right, creating excess demand at the old price. The price rises, which draws out more supply along the unchanged supply curve, so quantity also rises. A higher price with lower quantity would need a fall in supply, and the other options need a fall in demand or a rise in supply.

questions.stem_md: With the supply curve unchanged, a fall in the demand for mangoes in Ratnapuri at every price leads to

options.text_md: a higher equilibrium price and a smaller quantity
a lower equilibrium price and a smaller equilibrium quantity
a lower equilibrium price and a larger quantity
no change in either price or quantity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a lower equilibrium price and a smaller equilibrium quantity. A leftward shift of demand leaves excess supply at the old price. The price falls, and sellers move down their supply curve to a smaller quantity. The remaining options cannot follow from a shift of demand alone, since supply is unchanged.

questions.stem_md: A good harvest increases the supply of mangoes in Ratnapuri by 45 quintals at every price, with demand unchanged. The equilibrium price moves from Rs 20 to

options.text_md: Rs 15 per kg and quantity rises to 125 quintals
Rs 25 per kg and quantity rises to 120 quintals
Rs 15 per kg and quantity falls to 75 quintals
Rs 20 per kg and quantity rises to 145 quintals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Rs 15 per kg and quantity rises to 125 quintals. The new supply is 65 + 4p; equating it with 200 − 5p gives p = 15 and q = 125. The price falls and the quantity rises. The second option describes a rise in demand, the third gets the quantity wrong, and the last would need demand to rise as well.

questions.stem_md: A strike at the plants cuts the supply of cement in Sagarpur by 300 thousand bags at every price. If demand does not change, the equilibrium price becomes Rs 460 per bag. What happens to the quantity traded?

options.text_md: It rises to 720 thousand bags from 600
It falls to 420 thousand bags from 600
It stays at 600 thousand bags
It falls to 480 thousand bags, the result of a fall in demand

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It falls to 420 thousand bags from 600. Along the demand curve, quantity at the new price is 1800 − 3 × 460 = 420, a fall. A fall in supply cannot raise quantity, and quantity changes because the market moves along the demand curve. The figure 480 belongs to a fall in demand, not supply.

questions.stem_md: In Ratnapuri the demand for mangoes rises by 45 quintals at every price and the supply also rises by 45 quintals at every price. The new equilibrium price and quantity are

options.text_md: Rs 25 per kg and 120 quintals
Rs 15 per kg and 125 quintals
Rs 20 per kg and 145 quintals
Rs 20 per kg and 100 quintals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rs 20 per kg and 145 quintals. The new demand is 245 − 5p and the new supply is 65 + 4p, so 180 = 9p and p = 20, q = 145. The second option is the result of a rise in demand alone, the third of a rise in supply alone, and the last forgets that quantity rises.

questions.stem_md: Both the demand and the supply of mangoes in Ratnapuri rise, demand by 90 quintals and supply by 45 quintals at every price. Compared with Rs 20 per kg, the equilibrium price

options.text_md: falls, because supply has also risen
is unchanged, because both curves have shifted
falls to Rs 15, because the rise in demand is larger
rises to Rs 25, because the rise in demand is larger than the rise in supply

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** rises to Rs 25, because the rise in demand is larger than the rise in supply. When both curves shift right, the price rises if demand shifts more, and here the equilibrium is Rs 25. A rise in supply on its own lowers the price, but it is outweighed here. The price stays unchanged only if the two shifts are equal, and Rs 15 is the result if supply shifts more.

questions.stem_md: The demand for mangoes in Ratnapuri rises by 50 quintals at every price while a pest cuts supply by 40 quintals at every price. Starting from Rs 20 per kg and 100 quintals, the new equilibrium has

options.text_md: price Rs 20 per kg and the same quantity
price Rs 30 per kg and quantity 145 quintals
price Rs 25 per kg and quantity 75 quintals
price Rs 30 per kg and the same quantity of 100 quintals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** price Rs 30 per kg and the same quantity of 100 quintals. The new curves are 250 − 5p and -20 + 4p; they meet at p = 30, where the quantity is 250 − 5 × 30 = 100. The rise in demand lifts quantity and the fall in supply lowers it by the same amount, so quantity stays, while both shifts push price up. The other options mix up the cases.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following causes the demand curve for mangoes in Ratnapuri to shift to the right?

options.text_md: A fall in the price of mangoes
A rise in the price of mangoes
A rise in the incomes of Ratnapuri households, with mango a normal good
An increase in the number of mango sellers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A rise in the incomes of Ratnapuri households, with mango a normal good. A change in income, tastes or the prices of related goods shifts the demand curve. A change in the good’s own price is a movement along the same curve, and more sellers would shift the supply curve instead.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined weaving cluster of Kareempur, the wage per day settles at the level at which

options.text_md: every weaver is paid the same as the owner
the demand for weavers equals the supply of weavers
the demand for weavers is double the supply
employers pay as little as the law permits

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the demand for weavers equals the supply of weavers. A wage is the price of labour, and in a competitive labour market it is determined where labour demand equals labour supply. The other statements describe no equilibrium condition.

questions.stem_md: Suppose firms can enter and leave the cement industry of Sagarpur freely. In the long run, price in a perfectly competitive market tends to be equal to the

options.text_md: minimum average cost of a firm
maximum price buyers once paid
highest marginal cost of any firm
total fixed cost of the industry

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** minimum average cost of a firm. With free entry and exit, profits attract new firms and losses drive firms out, until price settles at the lowest point of the average cost curve. The other quantities have no such role.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined district of Chandanpur the administration fixes the highest price at which a cooking gas cylinder may be sold. Such a legal maximum is called a

options.text_md: price floor
price ceiling
support price
equilibrium price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** price ceiling. A price ceiling is a maximum price set by the government, normally below the equilibrium price. A floor is a minimum price, a support price is a kind of floor, and the equilibrium price emerges from the market rather than from a legal limit.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined district of Chandanpur (price p in Rs per cylinder, quantities in cylinders a week) households demand qd = 1200 − 1p and dealers supply qs = 0.5p. The administration fixes a ceiling of Rs 600 per cylinder. At this ceiling there is

options.text_md: a surplus of 300 cylinders a week
a shortage of 100 cylinders a week measured from equilibrium
neither shortage nor surplus
a shortage of 300 cylinders a week

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a shortage of 300 cylinders a week. At Rs 600 households demand 1200 − 600 = 600 cylinders, while dealers supply 0.5 × 600 = 300, so demand exceeds supply by 300. The gap is measured between demand and supply at the ceiling, which is what the third option gets wrong, and a ceiling below equilibrium cannot create a surplus.

questions.stem_md: The administration of Chandanpur, where the free market price of a cylinder is Rs 800, announces a ceiling of Rs 900. The most likely result is that the ceiling

options.text_md: has no effect, because the market price is already below it
creates a shortage of 150 cylinders
creates a surplus of 150 cylinders
forces the price up to the ceiling

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** has no effect, because the market price is already below it. A ceiling binds only when it is below the equilibrium price. At Rs 900 demand is 300 and supply is 450, so the market would drive price down to Rs 800 and the limit is never reached. Therefore it causes no shortage, and a ceiling cannot compel a rise in price.

questions.stem_md: When the supply of cooking gas cylinders in Chandanpur falls short of demand at a ceiling price, the administration may issue ration cards allowing each household a fixed number of cylinders. The purpose of rationing is to

options.text_md: raise the price above the ceiling
increase the quantity supplied beyond what dealers wish to sell
share the limited supply among households when price cannot do so
remove the shortage by reducing demand to zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** share the limited supply among households when price cannot do so. With price held down, it cannot ration the scarce good, so quotas and cards distribute it. Rationing does not raise the price or make dealers supply more, and it does not remove demand; the gap remains.

questions.stem_md: After a ceiling is imposed on cooking gas cylinders in Chandanpur, a shortage persists. Which development is a possible consequence?

options.text_md: The legal price automatically rises above the ceiling
All households receive as many cylinders as they want
Some cylinders are sold illegally above the ceiling to households willing to pay more
Dealers begin to supply more cylinders than before

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Some cylinders are sold illegally above the ceiling to households willing to pay more. Where legal supply is less than the quantity demanded, some buyers may pay more than the ceiling, which gives rise to a black market. The legal price cannot move above the ceiling, the shortage means not all demand is met, and a lower price does not draw out greater supply.

questions.stem_md: The government of the imagined district of Dhanpur announces a minimum price at which it will buy millet from farmers, set above the free market price. This is an example of a

options.text_md: price floor
price ceiling
rationing scheme
tax on farmers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** price floor. A price floor is a minimum price set by the government above the equilibrium price. A ceiling is a maximum price, a ration scheme limits quantities for buyers, and the announcement taxes nobody.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined millet market of Dhanpur (price p in Rs per kg, quantities in thousand kg a month) buyers demand qd = 500 − 4p and farmers supply qs = 100 + 6p. A floor of Rs 50 per kg is announced. At the floor price there is

options.text_md: a shortage of 100 thousand kg a month
a surplus of 40 thousand kg a month measured from the equilibrium quantity
no surplus, because farmers will not sell
a surplus of 100 thousand kg a month

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a surplus of 100 thousand kg a month. At Rs 50 buyers demand 500 − 4 × 50 = 300, while farmers supply 100 + 6 × 50 = 400, an excess supply of 100. A floor above equilibrium cannot produce a shortage, and the gap is read between supply and demand at the floor, not from the free-market quantity.

questions.stem_md: In the Dhanpur millet market, where the free market price is Rs 40 per kg, the government sets a minimum price of Rs 30 per kg. The effect of this floor is

options.text_md: a surplus of 100 thousand kg
none, because the market price is already above it
a surplus because supply exceeds demand at the floor
a fall in the market price to the floor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** none, because the market price is already above it. A floor matters only when it is above equilibrium. At Rs 30 demand is 380 and supply only 280, so excess demand lifts the price back to Rs 40, which is above the floor, and the floor is never reached. Hence a floor set so low produces no surplus.

questions.stem_md: The Dhanpur government buys the surplus of millet created by its minimum price and stores it. Grain held in this way by the government as a reserve is known as a

options.text_md: buffer stock
ration card
black market
price ceiling

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** buffer stock. A buffer stock is a reserve of the good that the government accumulates, here by buying the surplus at the floor price. A ration card is a coupon for buyers, a black market is illegal trade above a ceiling, and a ceiling is a maximum price.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined weaving cluster of Kareempur (wage w in Rs per day, quantities in numbers of weavers) employers demand 600 − 2w weavers and weavers offer −150 + 3w. A minimum wage of Rs 180 a day is enforced. At this wage

options.text_md: employers wish to hire 150 more weavers than are available
150 more weavers offer their labour than employers wish to hire
390 weavers are employed
the number of weavers employed is unchanged

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 150 more weavers offer their labour than employers wish to hire. Employers demand 600 − 2 × 180 = 240 weavers while 390 offer to work, so 150 more weavers are willing to work than are hired. Employment is the smaller number, 240, not 390, and it falls from 300, so it is not unchanged.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If the price in the Ratnapuri mango market is above the equilibrium price, the price tends to fall.

**Reason (R):** At a price above equilibrium the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, and sellers with unsold mangoes compete by lowering the price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. Excess supply leaves sellers with unsold stock, and underbidding by sellers drives the price down towards equilibrium.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An increase in the supply of mangoes in Ratnapuri, with demand unchanged, lowers the equilibrium price.

**Reason (R):** Mangoes are a seasonal fruit.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. The price falls because a rightward shift of supply creates excess supply at the old price; whether the fruit is seasonal plays no part in that argument.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If the demand and the supply of cement in Sagarpur both increase, the equilibrium price must rise.

**Reason (R):** An increase in demand alone raises the equilibrium price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false and R is true. With both curves shifting, the price may rise, fall or stay the same, depending on which shift is larger, so it does not have to rise.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A price ceiling fixed below the equilibrium price creates a shortage in the market.

**Reason (R):** At a price below the equilibrium price the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true and R is false. Below equilibrium it is the quantity demanded that exceeds the quantity supplied, which is why a binding ceiling produces a shortage.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A minimum price for millet fixed above the equilibrium price leaves farmers with unsold output unless the government buys it.

**Reason (R):** At the minimum price the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. The excess supply at the floor is exactly the output that buyers do not take, and it remains unsold unless bought by the government.

questions.stem_md: In the Deepgaon candle market, at a price of Rs 2 buyers demand 90 hundred candles and sellers supply 10. There is excess supply at this price.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Demand is larger than supply, so there is excess demand of 80 hundred candles, and the price will tend to rise.

questions.stem_md: A minimum price fixed below the equilibrium price has no effect on the quantity traded in a competitive market.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The market price is already above the floor, so the floor does not bind and nothing changes.

questions.stem_md: At the equilibrium price the quantity demanded is equal to the quantity ___.
questions.solution_md: Equilibrium has quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied.

questions.stem_md: A minimum price fixed by the government above the equilibrium price is called a price ___, and it creates excess ___.
questions.solution_md: A price floor above equilibrium leaves quantity supplied larger than quantity demanded, which is excess supply.

questions.stem_md: Match each term of market equilibrium with its meaning.

options.text_md: Equilibrium price
Excess demand
Excess supply
Equilibrium quantity

match_right.text_md: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a price
The quantity bought and sold at the equilibrium price
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a price

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The equilibrium price clears the market; excess demand and excess supply are the two kinds of gap away from it; the equilibrium quantity is the amount traded at the clearing price.

questions.stem_md: Match each event in an imagined market with its effect.

options.text_md: Demand rises, number of firms fixed
Supply rises, demand unchanged
Binding price ceiling
Binding price floor

match_right.text_md: Equilibrium price and quantity both rise
Equilibrium price falls and quantity rises

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A shift of demand to the right moves price and quantity together; a shift of supply to the right moves them in opposite directions; a ceiling opens a gap in favour of buyers and a floor opens one in favour of sellers.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps by which the Ratnapuri mango market moves to equilibrium when the price starts below the equilibrium price.

options.text_md: Excess demand shrinks until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: excess demand
Buyers compete for scarce mangoes and the price rises
The price is below the equilibrium price

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The sequence begins with a low price, which causes excess demand, which causes competition to raise the price, which narrows the gap until the market clears.

At the old price there is excess demand
The demand curve shifts to the right

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). The shift of demand opens a gap at the old price, price rises to close it, and the market settles at a new equilibrium.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the invisible hand in the adjustment of price to equilibrium? Use the mango market of Ratnapuri as an example.
questions.solution_md: Price adjusts without central direction.

answer.model_answer_md: The invisible hand is the idea that price moves to the market-clearing level through the separate choices of many buyers and sellers, with no authority directing them. In Ratnapuri, buyers bidding for scarce mangoes raise the price, and sellers with unsold mangoes lower it, until the two sides balance.

answer.model_answer_md: A price ceiling is a maximum price, fixed by the government, at which a good may be sold; it is meant to bind when it is below the equilibrium price. For example, Chandanpur fixes Rs 600 for a cooking gas cylinder when the free price would be Rs 800.

answer.model_answer_md: A price floor is a minimum price fixed by the government, below which a good may not be sold; it is meant to bind when set above the equilibrium price. For example, Dhanpur fixes Rs 50 per kg for millet when the free price would be Rs 40.

questions.stem_md: Describe three consequences of a ceiling of Rs 600 on cooking gas cylinders in Chandanpur, where the free price is Rs 800.
questions.solution_md: Shortage, rationing and queues, black market and quality.

answer.model_answer_md: First, a shortage of 300 cylinders a week appears, since demand is 600 and supply 300. Second, the scarce cylinders have to be shared by rationing, such as ration cards, or by queues. Third, a black market may arise, with some cylinders sold above the ceiling, and sellers may cut quality or service.

questions.stem_md: Describe three consequences of a floor of Rs 50 per kg in the millet market of Dhanpur, where the free price is Rs 40.
questions.solution_md: Surplus, purchase and storage, gainers and losers.

answer.model_answer_md: First, a surplus of 100 thousand kg a month appears, since supply is 400 and demand 300. Second, if the government buys the surplus, it must pay for it and store it as a buffer stock. Third, farmers gain a higher and more certain price, but buyers face a higher price and buy less than at equilibrium.

questions.stem_md: Why might a government fix a ceiling on essential goods or a floor on farm produce, and what problems may follow? Use imagined examples.

answer.model_answer_md: A ceiling on a necessity, such as cooking gas in Chandanpur, aims to keep it affordable for poorer households. A floor on millet in Dhanpur aims to protect farmers’ incomes. The problems are a shortage with queues and possible black markets under a ceiling, and a surplus that must be bought and stored under a floor.
